intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that auriculocondylar syndrome-4 (ARCND4) is caused by heterozygous duplication involving the HDAC9 gene (606543) on chromosome 7p21.1.

checks.claim: Auriculocondylar syndrome-4 (ARCND4) is caused by heterozygous duplication involving the HDAC9 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Our findings suggest that duplication of sequences at the HDAC9 locus can lead to the development of ARCND
checks.explanation: Paper supports a duplication involving HDAC9 causing ARCND; heterozygosity is implied by dominant segregation but not explicitly stated.

checks.claim: The HDAC9 gene is located on chromosome 7p21.1.
checks.evidence_quote: a tandem duplication of 430 kb in a candidate region on chromosome 7 defined by linkage analysis
checks.explanation: Chromosome 7 is stated; the band 7p21.1 is standard nomenclature, not stated in the paper.

paragraphs.text: Masotti et al. (2008) described auriculocondylar syndrome as an autosomal dominant disorder of the first and second pharyngeal arches. Its features are malformed 'question mark' ears, prominent cheeks, microstomia, an abnormal temporomandibular joint and hypoplasia of the mandibular condyle. They noted that penetrance seemed to be complete and that variability within and between families was high.

checks.evidence_quote: Auriculo-condylar syndrome (ACS), an autosomal dominant disorder of first and second pharyngeal arches

checks.claim: Features of auriculocondylar syndrome include malformed 'question mark' ears.
checks.evidence_quote: is characterized by malformed ears ('question mark ears')

checks.claim: Features of auriculocondylar syndrome include prominent cheeks.
checks.evidence_quote: malformed ears ('question mark ears'), prominent cheeks, microstomia

checks.claim: Features of auriculocondylar syndrome include microstomia.
checks.evidence_quote: prominent cheeks, microstomia, abnormal temporomandibular joint

checks.claim: Features of auriculocondylar syndrome include an abnormal temporomandibular joint.
checks.evidence_quote: microstomia, abnormal temporomandibular joint, and mandibular condyle hypoplasia

checks.claim: Features of auriculocondylar syndrome include hypoplasia of the mandibular condyle.
checks.evidence_quote: abnormal temporomandibular joint, and mandibular condyle hypoplasia

checks.claim: Penetrance of auriculocondylar syndrome seemed to be complete.
checks.evidence_quote: Penetrance seems to be complete

checks.claim: Auriculocondylar syndrome shows high intrafamilial and interfamilial variability.
checks.evidence_quote: there is high inter- and intra-familial phenotypic variation

paragraphs.text: Masotti et al. (2008) described a multigeneration family (F1) with 11 individuals affected by auriculocondylar syndrome. Clinical features varied within the family. Facial asymmetry, a feature not emphasized in earlier reports of the syndrome, was highly prevalent among the patients.

checks.claim: Facial asymmetry was not emphasized in earlier reports of auriculocondylar syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) studied a nonconsanguineous 4-generation Brazilian family (F1) with 11 members who had the typical features of ARCND. Of the documented members, 8 of 10 had question mark ears, 8 of 10 had microstomia and 6 of 10 had micrognathia. Intrafamilial variability was considerable. The patients did not have the large, open fontanelles seen in trisomy 7p.

checks.explanation: Four generations are stated elsewhere in the paper (abstract and Discussion).

paragraphs.text: Masotti et al. (2008) reported autosomal dominant inheritance of auriculocondylar syndrome in family F1. In the Brazilian family F1 reported by Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022), the disorder followed an autosomal dominant pattern and the causative duplication segregated with the phenotype. All unaffected family members tested negative for the duplication, which suggested full penetrance.

checks.evidence_quote: Auriculo-condylar syndrome (ACS), an autosomal dominant disorder of first and second pharyngeal arches
checks.explanation: The abstract calls ACS autosomal dominant in general and describes F1 as a multigeneration family. It does not explicitly say that the inheritance pattern in F1 was autosomal dominant.

checks.evidence_quote: Analysis parameters were defined as autosomal dominant, estimated penetrance K=0.9

paragraphs.text: Masotti et al. (2008) performed linkage analysis in 2 large auriculocondylar syndrome families. Segregation analysis excluded the loci for Treacher Collins syndrome, oculoauriculovertebral spectrum and Townes-Brocks syndrome. A genomewide search gave evidence of linkage to chromosome 1p21.1-q23.3 in family F2 (maximum lod score of 3.01 at theta = 0). This locus was not linked to the phenotype in family F1.

checks.evidence_quote: we conducted linkage analysis in two large ACS families, F1 and F2

checks.claim: Segregation analysis in the auriculocondylar syndrome families excluded the Treacher Collins syndrome locus.
checks.evidence_quote: Through segregation analysis, we first excluded three known loci associated with disorders of first and second pharyngeal arches (Treacher Collins syndrome, oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, and Townes-Brocks syndrome).

checks.claim: Segregation analysis in the auriculocondylar syndrome families excluded the oculoauriculovertebral spectrum locus.
checks.evidence_quote: Through segregation analysis, we first excluded three known loci associated with disorders of first and second pharyngeal arches (Treacher Collins syndrome, oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, and Townes-Brocks syndrome).

checks.claim: Segregation analysis in the auriculocondylar syndrome families excluded the Townes-Brocks syndrome locus.
checks.evidence_quote: Through segregation analysis, we first excluded three known loci associated with disorders of first and second pharyngeal arches (Treacher Collins syndrome, oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, and Townes-Brocks syndrome).

checks.claim: A genomewide search gave evidence of linkage of auriculocondylar syndrome to chromosome 1p21.1-q23.3 in family F2, with a maximum lod score of 3.01 at theta = 0.

checks.evidence_quote: Interestingly, this locus was not linked to the phenotype segregating in F1.

paragraphs.text: In a large Brazilian ARCND family, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) performed linkage analysis under an autosomal dominant model. They obtained a maximum lod score of 2.88, close to the theoretical maximum of 2.93 for the family, in a 17.6-Mb region on chromosome 7. Microsatellite genotyping narrowed the region to chr7:14395902-28158440 (hg38).

checks.evidence_quote: Analysis parameters were defined as autosomal dominant, estimated penetrance K=0.9, disease allele frequency estimated at 0.0001
checks.explanation: The linkage model was autosomal dominant.

checks.claim: Linkage analysis in the Brazilian ARCND family gave a maximum lod score of 2.88 in a 17.6-Mb region on chromosome 7.
checks.evidence_quote: The highest LOD score (2.88), which is close to the threshold value of ≥3.0 for significance and the maximum theoretical LOD score for this family (2.93), was observed in a region of about 17.6 Mb on chromosome 7

checks.claim: The theoretical maximum lod score for the Brazilian ARCND family was 2.93.
checks.evidence_quote: The maximum theoretical LOD score for this family was equal to 2.93.

checks.claim: Microsatellite genotyping narrowed the linked region in the Brazilian ARCND family to chr7:14395902-28158440 (hg38).
checks.evidence_quote: Genotyping of microsatellite markers narrowed the chromosome 7 linkage region to chr7:14395902–28158440 (hg38)

paragraphs.text: The auriculocondylar syndrome phenotype in family F1 was not linked to the ACS1 locus on chromosome 1p21.1-q23.3. Masotti et al. (2008) therefore concluded that at least 2 loci cause the phenotype.

paragraphs.text: TWIST1 was the top-ranked candidate gene in the linked region. In affected members of their Brazilian ARCND family, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) resequenced a 2.4-Mb region around TWIST1. They found no TWIST1 variants but detected a 430,302-bp tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) telomeric to TWIST1 that covered most of the HDAC9 gene. The duplication was predicted to duplicate several short HDAC9 isoforms entirely and to disrupt the full-length, catalytically active isoforms. Breakpoint amplification and Sanger sequencing showed that the duplication segregated with the phenotype (lod score of 2.88). All unaffected individuals tested negative.

checks.evidence_quote: We then took a gene prioritisation approach, and TWIST1 was the top-ranked gene in this analysis using two training lists

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) identified 19 patients in DECIPHER with copy-number gains in the region. Of these, 7 had ear malformations and 7 had micrognathia, and most of their duplications included the TWIST1 enhancer eTW6. One smaller duplication of 179 kb lay entirely within the ARCND duplication but did not include the TWIST1 regulatory elements. The patient carrying it had no features of ARCND.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) performed Capture-C in human embryonic calvarial mesenchymal cells, using the TWIST1 promoter as the viewpoint. Interactions were most frequent telomeric to TWIST1, within HDAC9 and the duplicated region, which implied that this region contains TWIST1 regulatory elements.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) derived neural crest cells from patient induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). These cells showed increased expression of HDAC9 (3.15-fold) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold) and a 4.3-fold reduction in migration, with no change in the cell cycle. Mesenchymal-like cells derived from the neural crest cells showed reduced alkaline phosphatase activity and expression and decreased matrix mineralization, indicating delayed or impaired osteogenic differentiation. The authors proposed that the duplication deregulates TWIST1 expression and causes ARCND by compromising neural crest migration and osteogenic differentiation. They suggested that patients may lack the large, open fontanelles of trisomy 7p because they carry 3 copies of regulatory elements rather than of the gene itself.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) studied a nonconsanguineous 4-generation Brazilian family with ARCND4. In affected members they identified a 430,302-bp tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) on chromosome 7, located telomeric to TWIST1, that covered most of the HDAC9 gene. The duplication segregated with the disorder (lod score of 2.88), and all unaffected family members tested negative. Capture-C showed that the duplicated region interacts with the TWIST1 promoter. Neural crest cells derived from patient iPSCs showed increased HDAC9 and TWIST1 expression and reduced migration. Mesenchymal-like cells derived from them showed impaired osteogenic differentiation.
